workingPaperSections.title: Project coordinator synthesis
workingPaperSections.body:
Project coordinator synthesis

What we know:
- The central question is minimal generation of two Schur families for the interval ideal \[ J_v\subseteq A=\Lambda/I_{r,q},\qquad Q=J_v/A_+J_v. \]
- Canonical accepted project work establishes the full parameter-uniform result: both \(G_L\) and \(G_R\) map to homogeneous integral bases of \(Q\), hence minimally generate \(J_v\).
- Consequently, \[ Q\cong\bigoplus_{\rho\subseteq b^a}\mathbb Z e_\rho,\qquad \deg e_\rho=ij+|\rho|,\qquad H_Q(z)=z^{ij}\binom{a+b}{a}_z. \] Thus \(Q\) is torsion-free and has a perfect degree-complement pairing.
- General coefficient formulas and explicit rank profiles for \(a=2\) and \(a=3\) are accepted consequences.
- Source-29 supports the lower-family theorem and no-syzygy mechanism. The right-family result is established internally through integral partition conjugation, not as a separately stated literature theorem.
- Accepted finite computations support several specializations, but they are not used to prove the general theorem.
- Accepted theorem-boundary consolidation research-plan-task-334 is finalized at its audited dependency boundary; claims outside that boundary are separate conjectures or future work.

Current roadblocks:
- The latest non-accepted task requires a bounded certificate repair: Compute or inspect representative small cases and look for structural obstructions.

CORRECTION REQUIRED IN THE REPLACEMENT OUTPUT:
Execute the genuinely new case \([2,2,2,0,0,0]\subseteq\lambda\subseteq[5,5,5,5,5,5]\) in every degree \(6,\ldots,30\), using \(h_1,\ldots,h_5\), with complete Pieri rows and verified integral witnesses \(U_dM_dV_d=D_d\); report degreewise quotient ranks, torsion, and any structural obstruction.
- No parameter-uniform formula for the \(G_L\)-to-\(G_R\) transition matrix is established. Accepted rank and torsion data cannot determine such matrices.
- The attempted larger-case transition computation lacks complete relation-lattice equality and explicit integral coordinate witnesses; its disputed matrices are not established.
- The task-313 determinant statement remains unavailable in persisted form, so reconstruction from adjacent source material is blocked.
- The latest proposed small example was mislabeled and duplicated the accepted \(i=j=p=2,c=3\) case; its partial computation supplied no new case.
- Open optional strengthenings do not alter or block the finalized theorem boundary.

115: \section{Introduction}
116: \label{intro-section}
117: %%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
118: 
119: %The first main result of this paper is Theorem 1.1 below.  We first
120: %explain here some of the background and motivation behind it.
121: % AY: I know we've talked about this before, but given there's an abstract,
122: % this sentence seems a little funny to me. What else were we planning to do
123: % but to explain the background and motivation for our result?
124: 
125: The cohomology of the generalized flag manifold $G/B$, for any complex
126: semisimple algebraic group $G$ and Borel subgroup $B$, has a classical
127: presentation due to Borel \cite{Borel}.  Pick a maximal torus
128: $T\subset B\subset G$, choose a field $\Bbbk$ of characteristic zero, and let
129: $V=\Bbbk\otimes_{\ZZ} X(T)$, where $X(T)$ is the coweight lattice of
130: $T$.  Let $\Bbbk[V]:=\Sym(V^{\star})$ be the symmetric algebra for
131: $V^{\star}$; it naturally carries an action of the Weyl group $W :=
132: N_G(T)/T$.  Furthermore let $\Bbbk[V]^W$ be the ring of $W$-invariants
133: of $\Bbbk[V]$, and $\Bbbk[V]^W_+$ the ideal of $\Bbbk[V]$ generated by
134: the $W$-invariants of positive degree.  A classical theorem of Borel
135: \cite{Borel} states that
136: \begin{equation}
137: \label{Borel-presentation}
138: H^*(G/B,\Bbbk) \cong \Bbbk[V]/(\Bbbk[V]^W_+).
139: \end{equation}
140: %This presentation is proved by showing that $\Bbbk[V]^W_+$ is the kernel of the
141: %surjective map $\Sym(V^\star) \rightarrow H^*(G/B)$ that sends a torus
142: %weight $\lambda \in V^{\star}$ to the first Chern class of the equivariant
143: %line bundle ${\mathcal L}_\lambda$ on $G/B$; see the original paper
144: %\cite{Borel} or, e.g., \cite[\S III.4]{Hiller} for further details.  
145: 
146: A desirable feature of Borel's presentation is its shortness: since $W$
147: acts on $V^\star$ as a finite reflection group, by Chevalley's Theorem,
148: the $W$-invariants $\Bbbk[V]^W$ are a polynomial algebra
149: $\Bbbk[f_1,\ldots,f_n]$, where $n:=\dim_\Bbbk V$ is the rank of
150: $G$ \cite[Section~3.5]{humphreys}.  Hence Borel's presentation shows
151: that $H^\star(G/B)$ is a complete intersection as it has $n$ generators and
152: $n$ relations.
153: 
154:  There is a second way to describe $H^{\star}(G/B)$ arising from
155:  a cell decomposition of $G/B$. One has
156: $$

198: 
199: This presentation \eqref{wasteful-presentation} involves a generating set \eqref{first-I-def}
200: for $I_w$ with at most $|W|$ generators.  However, this generating set
201: for $I_w$ is wasteful in that it not only generates $I_w$ as an ideal but
202: actually spans it $\Bbbk$-\emph{linearly} within $H^\star(G/B)$. 
203: 
204: Therefore, a basic question is to request more efficient generating
205: sets for $I_w$.  For type $A_{n-1}$, earlier work
206: \cite{GasharovReiner} reduced the $|W|=n!$ upper bound on the number
207: of generators for $I_w$ to a polynomial bound of $n^2$ for the class
208: of Schubert varieties $X_w$ \emph{defined by inclusions}; this class
209: includes all smooth $X_w$. Moreover, for a certain subclass of smooth
210: Schubert varieties $X_w$ considered originally by Ding
211: \cite{Ding1,Ding2}, they gave a smaller generating set for these $I_w$
212: having only $n$ generators.  This latter result was applied in
213: \cite{DevelinMartinReiner} to classify these varieties up to
214: isomorphism and homeomorphism (the generating set \eqref{first-I-def}
215: having proved too unwieldy). One motivation for this work arises from
216: the desire to extend this classification to general Schubert varieties of
217: type $A$.  Experience suggests that presentations for $I_w$ that are
218: as simple as possible are best for this purpose.
219: 
220: The question of finding 
221: simple presentations of $I_w$ for other root systems appears to 
222: have been less studied.
223: 
224: The main goal of this paper is to give a concise and root-system
225: uniform extension of Borel's presentation that produces for arbitrary
226: $w\in W$ an abbreviated list of generators for $I_w$.  Our first main
227: result, Theorem~\ref{general-bound}, achieves this via a strong
228: restriction on the {\bf descent set}
229: $$
230: \Des(u):=\{ s \in S: \ell(us) < \ell(u) \}
231: $$ of the elements $u$ in $W$ that index elements in our list of ideal
232: generators $\sigma_u$ for $I_w$.  We will need the following
233: definitions, the first two of which are standard:
234: \begin{enumerate}
235: \item[$\bullet$]
236: An element $u\in W$ is {\bf grassmannian} if $|\Des(u)| \leq 1$.

262: For any $w\in W$, working in a field $\Bbbk$ of characteristic zero,

3: ## Bibliographic identification
4: 
5: - **Title:** Presenting the cohomology of a Schubert variety
6: - **Authors:** Victor Reiner, Alexander Woo, Alexander Yong
7: - **arXiv:** [0809.2981v2](https://arxiv.org/abs/0809.2981v2)
8: - **Journal:** *Transactions of the American Mathematical Society* 363 (2011), 521–543
9: 
10: ## 1. The formally stated conjecture
11: 
12: ### Minimality conjecture
13: 
14: For a type-\(A_{n-1}\) bigrassmannian permutation \(v=v_{r,s,t,n}\), Theorem 5.4 supplies two generating sets for the ideal \(J_v\). The authors conjecture:
15: 
16: > **Conjecture.** The two generating sets for the ideal \(J_{v_{r,s,t,n}}\) given in Theorem 5.4 are both minimal.
17: 
18: Here, if \(\mathfrak S_v=s_{i^j}\), the parameters are
19: 
20: \[
21: a=\min(n-r-i,r-j),\qquad b=\min(i,j).
22: \]
23: 
24: Theorem 5.4 gives the two sets
25: 
26: \[
27: \{s_\mu:i^j\subseteq\mu\subseteq((i+a)^b,i^{j-b})\}
28: \]
29: 
30: and
31: 
32: \[
33: \{s_\mu:i^j\subseteq\mu\subseteq(i^j,b^a)\}.
### conjectures.md | SHA-256 6e74e126e04e50f43baed4b768113434e173637272f427fd8a3dcd8f3000ab02 | lines 41-110 | ordinary-document | excerpt SHA-256 44f553374621641c825a1615b82c6fe9d12c7561ec53f0e9c872901d4fd3a5ef
41: 
42: generators. “Minimal” means that no proper subset still generates \(J_v\).
43: 
44: **Primary-source location:** `sources/0809.2981v2.tex`, lines 1380–1421 and 1489–1499.
45: 
46: ## 2. Evidence reported by the authors
47: 
48: The authors state that they verified the conjecture computationally for all bigrassmannian permutations satisfying
49: 
50: \[
51: r\leq 4,\qquad n-r\leq 5.
52: \]
53: 
54: **Primary-source location:** lines 1501–1502.
55: 
56: ## 3. Stronger suspected formulation
57: 
58: Set \(M=J_{v_{r,s,t,n}}\), and let \(\Lambda_+\) denote the positive-degree part of the ring of symmetric functions. The authors further conjecture that
59: 
60: \[
61: M/\Lambda_+M
62: \]
63: 
64: requires \(\binom{a+b}{a}\) generators. They suspect the stronger structural statement
65: 
66: \[
67: M/\Lambda_+M\cong\mathbb Z^{\binom{a+b}{a}}.
68: \]
69: 
70: This is presented in prose rather than as a second numbered conjecture. The authors write that a proof had eluded them.
71: 
72: **Primary-source location:** lines 1517–1552.
73: 
74: ## 4. Consequence of the conjecture
75:

literatureSources.title: Model Reduction for Switched Differential-Algebraic Equations with Known Switching Signal
literatureSources.summary: Building on our recently proposed model reduction methods for switched ordinary linear systems, we propose a comprehensive model reduction method for linear switched differential-algebraic equations (DAEs). In contrast to most other available model reduction methods for switched systems, we consider the switching signal as a given time-variance of the system. This allows us to exploit certain linear subspaces in the reduction process and also provide in general significantly smaller reduced models compared to methods which consider arbitrary switching signals. Model reduction for switched DAEs has some unique features that make a generalization of the available methods nontrivial; in particular, the presence of jumps and Dirac impulses in response to switches have to be carefully treated. Furthermore, due to the algebraic constraints, the reachability subspaces cannot be the full space, hence a straightforward application of balanced truncation is not possible (because the corresponding reachability Gramians will be structurally non-invertible). We resolve this problem by first applying an exact model reduction which reduces the switched DAE to a switched ordinary system with jumps and which carefully keeps track of the impulsive effects. As a second step, we then apply a midpoint balanced truncation approach to further reduce the switched system. In addition to the challenge to appropriately take into account the Dirac impulses, another novel challenge was the occurrence of input-dependent state-jumps. We propose to deal with input-dependent jumps by combining certain discrete-time reachability Gramians with continuous-time reachability Gramians. We provide corresponding Matlab implementations of the proposed algorithms and illustrate their effectiveness with some academic examples.

literatureSources.summary: Animal social structure is influenced by demographic processes such as survival and recruitment. Yet, how the gain and loss of social associations among individuals scale up through levels of social organization is poorly understood. To address this gap, we conducted multiscale analysis of long-term social network dynamics over twelve winters for a migrant passerine, the golden-crowned sparrow. We found consistently high levels of stability in pairwise associations among returning sparrows, but this social fidelity was not the strongest driver of higher-level properties such as community cohesion and network modularity. Instead, these were increased more by the clustered social associations of newly immigrating individuals. Thus, the interplay of distinct processes---social fidelity among older birds and social cohesion among newer birds---jointly drive social structures at different levels of social organization. Our results demonstrate the different effects of demographic changes on social structure across pairwise, community, and population levels.

literatureSources.title: Blockchain Data Analytics: A Scoping Literature Review and Directions for Future Research
literatureSources.summary: Blockchain technology has rapidly expanded beyond its original use in cryptocurrencies to a broad range of applications, creating vast amounts of immutable, decentralized data. As blockchain adoption grows, so does the need for advanced data analytics techniques to extract insights for business intelligence, fraud detection, financial analysis and many more. While previous research has examined specific aspects of blockchain data analytics, such as transaction patterns, illegal activity detection, and data management, there remains a lack of comprehensive reviews that explore the full scope of blockchain data analytics. This study addresses this gap through a scoping literature review, systematically mapping the existing research landscape, identifying key topics, and highlighting emerging trends. Using established methodologies for literature reviews, we analyze 466 publications, clustering them into six major research themes: illegal activity detection, data management, financial analysis, user analysis, community detection, and mining analysis. Our findings reveal a strong focus on detecting illicit activities and financial applications, while holistic business intelligence use cases remain underexplored. This review provides a structured overview of blockchain data analytics, identifying research gaps and proposing future directions to enhance the fields impact.

literatureSources.title: Living Interactive Design: Towards Architectural Environments Responsive to User Biodata
literatureSources.summary:
In the modern era, technological advancements are progressing rapidly, leading to the emergence of a new 
concept in architectural design known as "Living Interactive Design." This approach aims to create 
intelligent and flexible architectural environments that respond directly to user data, thereby providing 
personalized experiences that enhance comfort and address individual needs. Living Interactive Design 
relies on collecting vital user data—such as heart rate, temperature, movement, and other environmental 
signals—and transforming this information into immediate environmental responses. For example, a 
building might adjust the lighting, temperature, or even music based on the user’s mood or activity. This 
paradigm represents a significant step toward developing smarter and more adaptable architectural 
environments, which continuously interact with users in real-time. It contributes to improving quality of 
life, increasing efficiency, and fostering human-environment interaction. Additionally, such designs 
facilitate energy consumption reduction and promote environmental sustainability through automatic 
adaptation to environmental conditions and changes in space usage. In summary, research in the field of 
Living Interactive Design seeks to offer innovative solutions that integrate technology and architecture, 
creating architectural environments that respond in a simple yet effective manner to user data. These 
environments aim to provide more personalized and flexible living experiences. This trend reflects a 
forward-looking vision based on ongoing, dynamic interaction between humans and their surrounding 
environment, opening new horizons toward more intelligent and sustainable architectural design.This study 
aims to explore and develop the concept of live interactive design for architectural environments that 
respond dynamically and instantly to users' vital data. To achieve this, an integrated methodology has been 
adopted, combining a review of scientific literature with the analysis of applied case studies, with the goal 
of building a comprehensive theoretical and practical framework that contributes to the development of 
design models based on live data.

literatureSources.title: Reduction of path integrals for interacting systems: The case of using dependent coordinates in the description of reduced motion on the orbit space
literatureSources.summary: We consider a reduction procedure in Wiener-type path integral for a finite-dimensional mechanical system with a symmetry representing the motion of two interacting scalar particles on a manifold that is the product of the total space of the principal bundle and a vector space. By analogy with what is done in gauge theories, the local description of the reduced motion on orbit space is carried out using dependent coordinates. The factorization of the measure in the path integral, which is necessary for the reduction, is based on the application of the stochastic differential equation of the optimal nonlinear filtering from the theory of stochastic processes. The non-invariance of the measure in the path integral under the reduction is shown. The Jacobian of the reduction is generated by the projection of the mean curvature vector field of the orbit onto the submanifold, which is used to determine the adapted coordinates in the principal fiber bundle associated with the problem under study.

literatureSources.title: <span>ALOGRITHIMIC CONTROL AND ECONOMIC DEPENDENCY IN PLATFORM BASED CORPORATIONS&nbsp;</span>
literatureSources.summary: <p><span>Platform based corporations have transformed the structure of work by substituting the past managerial control with algorithmic decision-making tools. Although such platforms present themselves as unbiased technological intermediaries, the algorithms are becoming important in determining essential elements of work, including the assignment of tasks, pricing, performance measurement, and even firing. This evolving model of governance poses essential questions about the character of control of such corporations and the corresponding economic dependency of platform workers.</span></p> <p><span>This paper discusses the issue of whether algorithmic control, which is formally portrayed to be technological facilitation, actually constitutes a substantive type of corporate control that defies the traditional separation between independent contracting and employment. Using the insights of company law theory and emergent labour and economic facts, the paper provides a study of the legal invisibility of dependency generated in platform-based work arrangements. The paper states that the lack of alignment between legal classification and functional reality create a need to redefine the issue of corporate responsibility in the digital economy. The study aims to add to the current discussion on regulation, governance, and the protection of vulnerable employees in algorithm-driven corporate entities through the use of doctrinal and analytical approaches.</span></p> <p><br></p>

literatureSources.title: Trajectory Data Management and Mining: A Survey from Deep Learning to the LLM Era
literatureSources.summary: Trajectory computing is a pivotal domain encompassing trajectory data management and mining, garnering widespread attention due to its crucial role in various practical applications such as location services, urban traffic, and public safety. Traditional methods, focusing on simplistic spatio-temporal features, face challenges of complex calculations, limited scalability, and inadequate adaptability to real-world complexities. In this paper, we present a comprehensive review of the development and recent advances in trajectory computing, from deep learning to the more recent large language models. We first define trajectory data and provide a brief overview of widely-used deep learning models. Systematically, we explore deep learning applications in trajectory management (pre-processing, storage, analysis, and visualization) and mining (trajectory-related forecasting, trajectory-related recommendation, trajectory classification, travel time estimation, anomaly detection, and mobility generation). Furthermore, we discuss emerging research directions and recent advancements in large models (represented by foundation models and large language models) for trajectory computing, which promise to reshape the next generation of trajectory computing. Additionally, we summarize application scenarios, public datasets, and toolkits. Finally, we outline current challenges in trajectory computing research and propose future directions. Relevant papers and open-source resources have been collated and are continuously updated at: https://github.com/yoshall/Awesome-Trajectory-Computing.

literatureSources.summary: The foreseen luminosity upgrade for the LHC (a factor of 5-10 more in peak luminosity by 2021) poses serious constraints on the technology for the ATLAS tracker in this High Luminosity era (HL-LHC). In fact, such luminosity increase leads to increased occupancy and radiation damage of the tracking detectors. To investigate the suitability of pixel sensors using the proven planar technology for the upgraded tracker, the ATLAS Planar Pixel Sensor R&D Project was established comprising 17 institutes and more than 80 scientists. Main areas of research are the performance of planar pixel sensors at highest fluences, the exploration of possibilities for cost reduction to enable the instrumentation of large areas, the achievement of slim or active edge designs to provide low geometric inefficiencies without the need for shingling of modules and the investigation of the operation of highly irradiated sensors at low thresholds to increase the efficiency. In the following I will present results from the group, concerning mainly irradiated-devices performance, together with studies for new sensors, including detailed simulations.

literatureSources.title: Presenting the cohomology of a Schubert variety: Proof of the minimality conjecture
literatureSources.venue: Journal of the London Mathematical Society
literatureSources.summary: Abstract A minimal presentation of the cohomology ring of the flag manifold was given in A. Borel (1953). This presentation was extended by E. Akyildiz–A. Lascoux–P. Pragacz (1992) to a nonminimal one for all Schubert varieties. Work of V. Gasharov–V. Reiner (2002) gave a short, that is, polynomial‐size, presentation for a subclass of Schubert varieties that includes the smooth ones. In V. Reiner–A. Woo–A. Yong (2011), a general shortening was found; it implies an exponential upper bound of on the number of generators required. That work states a minimality conjecture whose significance would be an exponential lower bound of on the number of generators needed in worst case, giving the first obstructions to short presentations. We prove the minimality conjecture. Our proof uses the Hopf algebra structure of the ring of symmetric functions.

20: Abstract.
21: We extend the short presentation due to [Borel ’53] of the cohomology
22: ring of a generalized flag manifold to a relatively short presentation
23: of the cohomology of any of its Schubert varieties. Our result is
24: stated in a root-system uniform manner by introducing the essential set of a Coxeter group element , generalizing and giving a
25: new characterization of [Fulton ’92]’s definition for permutations.
26: Further refinements are obtained in type A.
27: Key words and phrases:
28: Schubert calculus, Schubert variety, cohomology presentation, bigrassmannian, essential set
29: 2000 Mathematics Subject Classification:
30: 14M15, 14N15
31: 1. Introduction
32: The cohomology of the generalized flag manifold G/B, for any complex
33: semisimple algebraic group G and Borel subgroup B, has a classical
34: presentation due to Borel [ B53 ] . Pick a maximal torus
35: T\subset B\subset G, choose a field \Bbbk of characteristic zero, and let
36: V=\Bbbk\otimes_{{\mathbb{Z}}}X(T), where X(T) is the coweight lattice of
37: T. Let \Bbbk[V]:=\mathrm{Sym}(V^{\star}) be the symmetric algebra for
38: V^{\star}; it naturally carries an action of the Weyl group W:=N_{G}(T)/T. Furthermore let \Bbbk[V]^{W} be the ring of W-invariants
39: of \Bbbk[V], and \Bbbk[V]^{W}_{+} the ideal of \Bbbk[V] generated by
40: the W-invariants of positive degree. A classical theorem of Borel
41: [ B53 ] states that
42: (1.1)
43: H^{*}(G/B,\Bbbk)\cong\Bbbk[V]/(\Bbbk[V]^{W}_{+}).
44: A desirable feature of Borel’s presentation is its shortness: since W
45: acts on V^{\star} as a finite reflection group, by Chevalley’s Theorem,
46: the W-invariants \Bbbk[V]^{W} are a polynomial algebra
47: \Bbbk[f_{1},\ldots,f_{n}], where n:=\dim_{\Bbbk}V is the rank of
48: G [ H90 , Section 3.5] . Hence Borel’s presentation shows
49: that H^{\star}(G/B) is a complete intersection as it has n generators and
50: n relations.
51: There is a second way to describe H^{\star}(G/B) arising from
52: a cell decomposition of G/B. One has
53: \begin{array}[]{rll}G&=\bigsqcup_{w\in W}BwB&\text{(Bruhat decomposition)}\\
54: G/B&=\bigsqcup_{w\in W}X_{w}^{\circ}&\text{(Schubert cell decomposition), with}\\
55: X_{w}^{\circ}&:=BwB/B\cong{\mathbb{C}}^{\ell(w)}&\text{ (open Schubert cell)}.\end{array}
56: Here \ell(w) denotes the Coxeter group length of w under the
57: Coxeter system (W,S), where S are the reflections in the simple
58: roots \Pi among the positive roots \Phi^{+}
59: within the natural root system \Phi associated to our Lie pinning.
60: This gives a
61: CW-decomposition for G/B in which all cells have even real
62: dimension. Hence the fundamental homology classes [X_{w}] of their
63: closures X_{w}:=\overline{X_{w}^{\circ}}, the Schubert varieties ,
64: form a {\mathbb{Z}}-basis for the integral homology H_{\star}(G/B), and their
65: (Kronecker) duals \sigma_{w}:=[X_{w}]^{\star} form the dual {\mathbb{Z}}-basis for
66: the integral cohomology H^{\star}(G/B).
67: The above facts lead to an a priori presentation
68: for H^{\star}(X_{w}); see also [ C92 , Cor. 4.4] and
69: [ GR02 , Prop. 2.1] : The Schubert variety X_{w} is the
70: union of the Schubert cells X_{u}^{\circ} for which u\leq w in the
71: (strong) Bruhat order ; hence it inherits a cell decomposition
72: from the flag variety. Consequently, the map on cohomology
73: H^{\star}(G/B)\rightarrow H^{\star}(X_{w})
74: induced by including X_{w}\hookrightarrow G/B is surjective
75: with kernel
76: (1.2)
77: I_{w}:=\Bbbk\text{-span of }\{\sigma_{u}:u\not\leq w\}.
78: This gives rise to presentations
79: (1.3)
80: \displaystyle H^{\star}(X_{w})
81: \displaystyle\cong H^{\star}(G/B)/I_{w}
82: \displaystyle\text{ working over }{\mathbb{Z}}
83: \displaystyle\cong\Bbbk[V]/\left(I_{w}+\Bbbk[V]^{W}_{+}\right)
84: \displaystyle\text{ working over }\Bbbk.
85: This presentation ( 1.3 ) involves a generating set ( 1.2 )
86: for I_{w} with at most |W| generators. However, this generating set
87: for I_{w} is wasteful in that it not only generates I_{w} as an ideal but
88: actually spans it \Bbbk- linearly within H^{\star}(G/B).
89: Therefore, a basic question is to request more efficient generating
90: sets for I_{w}. For type A_{n-1}, earlier work
91: [ GR02 ] reduced the |W|=n! upper bound on the number
92: of generators for I_{w} to a polynomial bound of n^{2} for the class
93: of Schubert varieties X_{w} defined by inclusions ; this class
94: includes all smooth X_{w}. Moreover, for a certain subclass of smooth
95: Schubert varieties X_{w} considered originally by Ding
96: [ D97 , D01 ] , they gave a smaller generating set for these I_{w}
97: having only n generators. This latter result was applied in
98: [ DMR07 ] to classify these varieties up to
99: isomorphism and homeomorphism (the generating set ( 1.2 )
100: having proved too unwieldy). One motivation for this work arises from
101: the desire to extend this classification to general Schubert varieties of
102: type A. Experience suggests that presentations for I_{w} that are
103: as simple as possible are best for this purpose.
104: The question of finding
105: simple presentations of I_{w} for other root systems appears to
106: have been less studied.
107: The main goal of this paper is to give a concise and root-system
108: uniform extension of Borel’s presentation that produces for arbitrary
109: w\in W an abbreviated list of generators for I_{w}. Our first main
110: result, Theorem 1.1 , achieves this via a strong
111: restriction on the descent set
112: \mathrm{Des}(u):=\{s\in S:\ell(us) \bullet
113: An element u\in W is grassmannian if |\mathrm{Des}(u)|\leq 1.
114: \bullet
115: An element v\in W is bigrassmannian if both v and v^{-1} are grassmannian.
116: \bullet
117: Given w\in W, the essential set for w, denoted
118: {\mathcal{E}}(w), is the set of u\in W which are minimal in the Bruhat order among those
119: not below w.
120: The nomenclature “essential set” for {\mathcal{E}}(w) is justified in
121: Proposition 4.6 , where we give a new
122: characterization of Fulton’s essential set [ F92 ] for the case
123: of the symmetric group W=S_{n}. Indeed, {\mathcal{E}}(w) has been
124: previously studied from a different point of view: a result of Lascoux
125: and Schützenberger [ LS96 , Théorème 3.6] ,
126: implicit in
127: our first main result below, is that the elements in
128: {\mathcal{E}}(w) are bigrassmannian for any w in W. 1 1 1 For Lascoux
129: and Schützenberger this arises in their work (see also Geck and Kim
130: [ GK97 ] and Reading [ R02 ] ) seeking efficient encodings of the strong Bruhat order; it is perhaps not surprising that
131: it should arise in our search for efficient cohomology presentations
132: as well.
133: Theorem 1.1 .
134: For any w\in W, working in a field \Bbbk of characteristic zero,
135: the ideal I_{w} defining H^{\star}(X_{w}) as a quotient of H^{\star}(G/B) is
136: generated by the cohomology classes \sigma_{u} where u\not\leq w
137: and u is grassmannian.
138: More precisely, I_{w} is generated by the classes \sigma_{u} indexed
139: by those grassmannian u for which there exist some bigrassmannian
140: v in {\mathcal{E}}(w) satisfying both u\geq v and \mathrm{Des}(u)=\mathrm{Des}(v).
141: In type A, a similar result was obtained by Akyildiz, Lascoux, and
142: Pragacz [ ALP92 , Theorem 2.2] . Specifically, they prove the first
143: sentence of Theorem 1.1 , though they do not address the
144: strengthening given by the second sentence. Their methods are mainly
145: geometric, as opposed to our essentially combinatorial arguments. Their
146: work provides, to our knowledge, the first inroads towards an abbreviated
147: generating set for I_{w}.

212: 2. Proof of Theorem 1.1

545: \{S_{u}\} for those u for which there exist v\in{\mathcal{E}}(w_{\max}) satisfying both u\geq v and \mathrm{Des}(u)\subseteq\mathrm{Des}(v). By (i), this forces u to lie in W^{J}, so that S_{u} is
546: W^{J}-invariant and therefore lies in R.
547: For assertion (iii), from the definition
548: ( 3.4 ) and the fact that R has a
549: \Bbbk-basis given by \{S_{u}:u\in W^{J}\}, it suffices to show that
550: for any u in W^{J}, one has uW_{J}\leq wW_{J} if and only if u\leq w_{\max}. By definition, uW_{J}\leq wW_{J} if and only if u\leq w_{\min}, where w_{\min} is the unique representative of wW_{J}
551: lying in W^{J}. The usual parabolic factorization W=W^{J}\cdot W_{J}
552: allows one to write down a reduced word \omega for w_{\max} in the
553: concatenated form
554: \omega=\omega_{1}\cdot\omega_{2}
555: where the prefix \omega_{1} factors w_{\min}, and the suffix
556: \omega_{2} contains only generators in J. The subword
557: characterization of Bruhat order [ BB05 , Cor. 2.2.3]
558: shows that u\leq w_{\max} if and only if u is factored by a
559: reduced subword of this word \omega; this subword must necessarily use no
560: generators from J (since u is in W^{J}) and hence must actually be a
561: subword of \omega_{1}. Thus u\leq w_{\max} if and only if u\leq w_{\min}, as desired.
562: Assertion (iv) then follows from assertions (ii), (iii) and Proposition 3.1 .
563: ∎
564: 4. Refinements in Type A
565: We investigate further the situation when W is a Weyl group of
566: type A_{n-1}, which exhibits extra features; one can:
567: \bullet
568: be more explicit about bigrassmannians and their essential sets {\mathcal{E}}(w),
569: \bullet
570: produce even smaller generating sets for the ideals
571: I_{w} and J_{v}, which are conjecturally minimal in the case of J_{v}, and
572: \bullet
573: work with {\mathbb{Z}} coefficients rather than
574: over a field \Bbbk of characteristic zero.
575: 4.1. Schubert conditions and bigrassmannians
576: In type A_{n-1}, points in the variety G/B
577: are identified with complete flags of subspaces
578: \langle 0\rangle\subset V_{1}\subset\cdots\subset V_{n-1}\subset{\mathbb{C}}^{n}
579: having \dim_{\mathbb{C}}V_{i}=i. Pick as our particular base flag \{{\mathbb{C}}^{i}\}_{i=0}^{n}, where {\mathbb{C}}^{i} is spanned by the first i standard
580: basis elements; this flag is fixed by the Borel subgroup B
581: consisting of the invertible upper-triangular matrices within
582: G:=GL_{n}({\mathbb{C}}). Picking the maximal torus T of invertible diagonal
583: matrices, one identifies the Weyl group W=N_{G}(T)/T with the
584: symmetric group S_{n}. The Coxeter generators S for W=S_{n}
585: associated to our Borel subgroup B is the set of adjacent
586: transpositions S=\{(1\leftrightarrow 2),(2\leftrightarrow 3),\ldots,(n-1\leftrightarrow n)\}.
587: The Schubert variety X_{w} corresponding to a
588: permutation w=w_{1}w_{2}\cdots w_{n}\in S_{n} (written in one-line notation)
589: can be defined as the subvariety
590: of flags satisfying the conjunction of the Schubert conditions
591: (4.1)
592: \dim_{\mathbb{C}}(V_{r}\cap{\mathbb{C}}^{s})\geq t
593: where
594: (4.2)
595: t={t}_{r,s}(w):=|\{w_{1},w_{2},\ldots,w_{r}\}\cap\{1,2,\ldots,s\}|
596: for all r,s=1,2,\ldots,n-1 is the rank function associated to w.
597: Denote the condition ( 4.1 )
598: by C_{r,s,t} (for arbitrary t, not necessarily of the form ( 4.2 )).
599: Note that C_{r,s,t} is vacuous unless t>r+s-n.
600: The following
601: explicit identification of bigrassmannian permutations
602: is well-known and straightforward.
603: Lemma 4.1 .
604: The bigrassmannian permutations (other than the identity) are
605: parameterized by r,s,t with 1\leq t\leq r,s\leq n and t>r+s-n.
606: Let v_{r,s,t,n} denote the unique bigrassmannian permutation
607: v_{1}\ldots v_{n}\in S_{n} such that
608: \bullet
609: \mathrm{Des}(v)=\{(r\leftrightarrow r+1)\}
610: \bullet
611: \mathrm{Des}(v^{-1})=\{(s\leftrightarrow s+1)\} , and
612: \bullet
613: v_{t}=s+1 .
614: Then explicitly we have:
615: (4.3)
616: \displaystyle v_{r,s,t,n}
617: \displaystyle:=(1,2,\ldots,t-1,
618: \displaystyle\qquad s+1,s+2,\ldots,s+r-t+1,
619: \displaystyle\quad\qquad t,t+1,t+2,\ldots,s,
620: \displaystyle\qquad\qquad s+r-t+2,s+r-t+3,\ldots,n).
621: There is a simple relation between these Schubert conditions C_{r,s,t}
622: and the bigrassmannian permutations in W=S_{n}:
623: Proposition 4.2 .
624: Let w\in S_{n}.
625: Then the Schubert condition C_{r,s,t} is satisfied by all flags in X_{w}
626: if and only if v_{r,s,t,n}\not\leq w.
627: Proof.
628: Note C_{r,s,t} is a Schubert condition on X_{w} if and only
629: if t_{r,s}(w)\geq t. It is then straightforward to check that the latter is
630: equivalent to v_{r,s,t,n}\not\leq w using the tableau criterion
631: [ BB05 , Theorem 2.6.3] for comparing elements in the Bruhat ordering.
632: ∎
633: Note that imposing an arbitrary conjunction of Schubert conditions on
634: complete flags cuts out a B-stable subvariety of G/B,
635: but this subvariety may be a reducible
636: union of Schubert varieties rather than a single Schubert variety X_{w}.
637: However, in type A, when one imposes a single Schubert condition, the result is
638: always a (single) Schubert variety. This fact can be
639: traced to special properties of the Bruhat order in type A,
640: first identified by Lascoux and Schützenberger [ LS96 ] ,
641: and exploited further by Geck and Kim [ GK97 ] and Reading [ R02 ] .
642: To explain this, we first recall some terminology.
643: Definition 4.3 .
644: In a poset P, say that an element v is a dissector of P if
645: there exists a (necessarily unique) element w in P for which P
646: decomposes as the disjoint union of the principal order filter above v and the
647: principal order ideal below w:
648: P=\{u\in P:u\geq v\}\quad\bigsqcup\quad\{u\in P:u\leq w\}.
649: Say that an element a in a poset P (which need not be a lattice) is
650: join-irreducible
651: if there does not exist a subset X\subset P with a\not\in X
652: such that a is the least element among all upper bounds for X in P.
653: There are two subtle issues to point out in this definition of
654: join-irreducibles. Firstly, when the finite poset is a lattice , an element
655: is join-irreducible if and only if it covers a unique element.
656: However, for non-lattices, one can have join-irreducibles
657: that cover more than one element.
658: For example, the strong Bruhat order in type A_{2} has four non-minimal, non-maximal elements,
659: each of which is join-irreducible, but two of them cover two elements.
660: Secondly, all of the posets that we will consider have a unique least element,
661: (e.g. in Bruhat order on W, the least element is the identity of W), and this least element
662: is not considered join-irreducible because it is the least element among all upper
663: bounds for the empty set X=\varnothing.
664: Theorem 4.4 .
665: [ LS96 , GK97 , R02 ]
666: (i)
667: In any finite poset, every dissector is join-irreducible. When the
668: poset is the Bruhat order for a Coxeter system (W,S) of type A,B,H_{3},H_{4} or
669: I_{2}(m) , the converse holds: the join-irreducible elements are exactly the dissectors.
670: (ii)
671: In the Bruhat order for any finite Coxeter system (W,S) , every join-irreducible element is bigrassmannian.
672: In type A , the converse holds: the (non-identity) bigrassmannian elements are exactly the join-irreducibles.
673: In particular, in type A, for every bigrassmannian v in W, there exists a (necessarily unique) element
674: w in W for which {\mathcal{E}}(w)=\{v\}.
675: Corollary 4.5 .
676: In type A_{n-1}, a single Schubert condition C_{r,s,t} on the flags
677: in G/B cuts out the Schubert variety X_{w_{r,s,t,n}} in G/B, where
678: w_{r,s,t,n} is the unique element with {\mathcal{E}}(w_{r,s,t,n})=\{v_{r,s,t,n}\}
679: as in Theorem 4.4 .
680: Thus in type A_{n-1}, for any bigrassmannian
681: v_{r,s,t,n}, one has equality of
682: the two ideals J_{v_{r,s,t,n}}=I_{w_{r,s,t,n}} within the coinvariant algebra
683: \Bbbk[V]/(\Bbbk[V]^{W}_{+}).
684: We remark that, as with v_{r,s,t,n}, one knows w_{r,s,t,n} explicitly
685: (see [ R02 , §8] ):
686: \displaystyle w_{r,s,t,n}
687: \displaystyle=(n,n-1,\ldots,(n-r+t+1),
688: \displaystyle\qquad s,s-1,\ldots,s-t+1,
689: \displaystyle\quad\qquad n-r+t,n-r+t-3,\ldots,s+1,
690: \displaystyle\qquad\qquad s-t,s-t-1,\ldots,1).
691: 4.2. Bigrassmannians and essential Schubert conditions
692: Next, we explain the relation between what we have called the essential set {\mathcal{E}}(w)
693: for w and Fulton’s essential set of Schubert conditions for X_{w}.
694: Note that there are implications among the various Schubert conditions C_{r,s,t}.
695: Fulton introduced the essential set of a permutation, a set of coordinates
696: \{(r_{i},s_{i})\}\subset n\times n which give an inclusion-minimal subset of
697: Schubert conditions C_{r_{i},s_{i},t} with t=t_{r_{i},s_{i}}(w) that suffice to define
698: X_{w} as a subset of the flag manifold. (See further remarks in Example 4.7
699: below.) Correspondingly, we call these Schubert conditions the
700: essential Schubert conditions for
701: X_{w}; see [ F92 , §3] , [ FP98 , pp. 20-21] , and
702: [ EL96 , §2] .
703: Proposition 4.6 .
704: The Schubert condition C_{r,s,t} implies the Schubert condition C_{r^{\prime},s^{\prime},t^{\prime}}
705: if and only if v_{r,s,t,n}\leq v_{r^{\prime},s^{\prime},t^{\prime},n} in Bruhat order.
706: Therefore in type A_{n-1}, Fulton’s essential set of Schubert conditions C_{r,s,t} for X_{w}
707: correspond bijectively to the elements of the essential set {\mathcal{E}}(w) for w defined for a general
708: Coxeter group.
709: Proof.
710: For the first assertion, note that the Schubert cell decomposition for X_{w} and
711: Theorem 4.4 give the following:
712: \displaystyle C_{r,s,t}\text{ implies }C_{r^{\prime},s^{\prime},t^{\prime}}\Leftrightarrow
713: \displaystyle\qquad X_{w_{r,s,t,n}}\subseteq X_{w_{r^{\prime},s^{\prime},t^{\prime},n}}
714: \displaystyle\Leftrightarrow
715: \displaystyle\qquad\{u\in W:u\leq w_{r,s,t,n}\}\subseteq\{u\in W:u\leq w_{r^{\prime},s^{\prime},t^{\prime},n}\}
716: \displaystyle\Leftrightarrow
717: \displaystyle\qquad\{u\in W:u\geq v_{r,s,t,n}\}\supseteq\{u\in W:u\geq v_{r^{\prime},s^{\prime},t^{\prime},n}\}
718: \displaystyle\Leftrightarrow
719: \displaystyle\qquad v_{r,s,t,n}\leq v_{r^{\prime},s^{\prime},t^{\prime},n}.
720: The second assertion follows immediately from the first.
721: ∎

943: The two generating sets for the ideal J_{v_{r,s,t,n}} given in Theorem 4.8
944: are both minimal.
945: Via computer, we have verified this conjecture for all bigrassmannian permutations

948: H^{\star}(X_{w}) in general. We now give
949: a family of ideals that would require a large number of generators if the conjecture is true.

955: generators according to Conjecture 4.10 .
956: The size of any minimal generating set of a homogeneous ideal is
957: well-defined. This is implied by the following well-known fact:
958: Proposition 4.11 .
959: Let R be a commutative ring, and \Lambda=\oplus_{n\geq 0}\Lambda_{n} a graded, connected R-algebra, meaning that \Lambda_{0}=R and \Lambda_{i}\Lambda_{j}\subset\Lambda_{i+j}. Let M be a
960: graded \Lambda-module, with degrees bounded below, meaning that
961: M=\oplus_{n\geq N}M_{n} for some N\in{\mathbb{Z}}, and \Lambda_{i}M_{j}\subset M_{i+j}.
962: Then a set of homogeneous elements \{m_{i}\}_{i=1}^{t} generate M as a \Lambda-module
963: if and only if their images \{\bar{m_{i}}\}_{i=1}^{t} span M/\Lambda_{+}M as a R-module.
964: In particular, \{m_{i}\}_{i=1}^{t} form a minimal \Lambda-generating set with respect to
965: inclusion for M if and only if \{\bar{m_{i}}\}_{i=1}^{t} form a minimal R-spanning
966: set for M/\Lambda_{+}M.
967: In our setting, the well-definedness follows by setting
968: \Lambda=\oplus_{n\geq 0}\Lambda_{n} to be the graded ring of
969: symmetric functions with {\mathbb{Z}} coefficients and setting
970: M=J_{v_{r,s,t,n}}, so that the {\mathbb{Z}}-module M/\Lambda_{+}M
971: is a finitely generated abelian group.
972: Thus we conjecture that this abelian group M/\Lambda_{+}M requires
973: \binom{a+b}{a} generators, and in fact, we suspect that
974: M/\Lambda_{+}M\cong{\mathbb{Z}}^{\binom{a+b}{a}}. So far a proof
975: has eluded us.

literatureSources.title: Presenting the cohomology of a Schubert variety
literatureSources.summary: We extend the short presentation due to [Borel '53] of the cohomology ring of a generalized flag manifold to a relatively short presentation of the cohomology of any of its Schubert varieties. Our result is stated in a root-system uniform manner by introducing the essential set of a Coxeter group element, generalizing and giving a new characterization of [Fulton '92]'s definition for permutations. Further refinements are obtained in type A.

literatureSources.title: Schur Polynomials and Plücker degree of Schubert Varieties
literatureSources.summary: The polynomial ring $B$ in infinitely many indeterminates $(x_1,x_2,\ldots)$, with rational coefficients, has a vector space basis of Schur polynomials, parametrized by partitions. The goal of this note is to provide an explanation of the following fact. If $\blamb$ is a partition of weight $d$, then the partial derivative of order $d$ with respect to $x_1$ of the Schur polynomial $S_\blamb(\bfx)$ coincides with the Plücker degree of the Schubert variety of dimension $d$ associated to $\blamb$, equal to the number of standard Young tableaux of shape $\blamb$. The generating function encoding all the degree of Schuberte varieties is determined and some (known) corollaries are also discussed. (The following is an informal report on the contributed talk given by the author during the INPANGA 2020[+1] meeting on Schubert Varieties.)

literatureSources.title: Ultralight vector dark matter search using data from the KAGRA O3GK run
authors: J. F. J. van den Brand
M. H. P. M. van Putten
literatureSources.summary: Among the various candidates for dark matter (DM), ultralight vector DM can be probed by laser interferometric gravitational wave detectors through the measurement of oscillating length changes in the arm cavities. In this context, KAGRA has a unique feature due to differing compositions of its mirrors, enhancing the signal of vector DM in the length change in the auxiliary channels. Here we present the result of a search for $U(1)_{B-L}$ gauge boson DM using the KAGRA data from auxiliary length channels during the first joint observation run together with GEO600. By applying our search pipeline, which takes into account the stochastic nature of ultralight DM, upper bounds on the coupling strength between the $U(1)_{B-L}$ gauge boson and ordinary matter are obtained for a range of DM masses. While our constraints are less stringent than those derived from previous experiments, this study demonstrates the applicability of our method to the lower-mass vector DM search, which is made difficult in this measurement by the short observation time compared to the auto-correlation time scale of DM.

literatureSources.title: Cohomology ring of the flag variety vs Chow cohomology ring of the Gelfand–Zetlin toric variety
literatureSources.summary: We compare the cohomology ring of the flag variety {\mathcal{F}\ell}_n and the Chow cohomology ring of the Gelfand–Zetlin toric variety X_{\operatorname{GZ}} .We show that H^*(\mathcal{F}{\ell}_n, \mathbb{Q}) is the Poincaré duality quotient of the subalgebra of A^*(X_{\operatorname{GZ}}, \mathbb{Q}) generated by degree 1 elements. We compute these algebras for n=3 and see that, in general, this subalgebra does not have Poincaré duality.

literatureSources.title: Torus fixed point sets of Hessenberg Schubert varieties in regular semisimple Hessenberg varieties
literatureSources.summary: It is well-known that the $T$-fixed points of a Schubert variety in the flag variety $GL_n(\mathbb{C})/B$ can be characterized purely combinatorially in terms of Bruhat order on the symmetric group $\mathfrak{S}_n$. In a recent preprint, Cho, Hong, and Lee give a combinatorial description of the $T$-fixed points of Hessenberg analogues of Schubert varieties (which we call Hessenberg Schubert varieties) in a regular semisimple Hessenberg variety. This note gives an interpretation of their result in terms of Bruhat order by making use of a partition of the symmetric group defined using so-called subsets of Weyl type. The Appendix, written by Michael Zeng, proves a lemma concerning subsets of Weyl type which is required in our arguments.

literatureSources.title: Deep Search for Joint Sources of Gravitational Waves and High-Energy Neutrinos with IceCube During the Third Observing Run of LIGO and Virgo
authors: J. F. J. van den Brand
M. H. P. M. van Putten
literatureSources.summary: The discovery of joint sources of high-energy neutrinos and gravitational waves has been a primary target for the LIGO, Virgo, KAGRA, and IceCube observatories. The joint detection of high-energy neutrinos and gravitational waves would provide insight into cosmic processes, from the dynamics of compact object mergers and stellar collapses to the mechanisms driving relativistic outflows. The joint detection of multiple cosmic messengers can also elevate the significance of the common observation even when some or all of the constituent messengers are sub-threshold, i.e. not significant enough to declare their detection individually. Using data from the LIGO, Virgo, and IceCube observatories, including sub-threshold events, we searched for common sources of gravitational waves and high-energy neutrinos during the third observing run of Advanced LIGO and Advanced Virgo detectors. Our search did not identify significant joint sources. We derive constraints on the rate densities of joint sources. Our results constrain the isotropic neutrino emission from gravitational-wave sources for very high values of the total energy emitted in neutrinos (> $10^{52} - 10^{54}$ erg).

literatureSources.title: Presenting the cohomology of a Schubert variety: Proof of the minimality conjecture
literatureSources.summary: A minimal presentation of the cohomology ring of the flag manifold $GL_n/B$ was given in [A. Borel, 1953]. This presentation was extended by [E. Akyildiz-A. Lascoux-P. Pragacz, 1992] to a non-minimal one for all Schubert varieties. Work of [Gasharov-Reiner, 2002] gave a short, i.e. polynomial-size, presentation for a subclass of Schubert varieties that includes the smooth ones. In [V. Reiner-A. Woo-A. Yong, 2011], a general shortening was found; it implies an exponential upper bound of $2^n$ on the number of generators required. That work states a minimality conjecture whose significance would be an exponential lower bound of $\sqrt{2}^{n+2}/\sqrt{πn}$ on the number of generators needed in worst case, giving the first obstructions to short presentations. We prove the minimality conjecture. Our proof uses the Hopf algebra structure of the ring of symmetric functions.

250: denoted \nu/\lambda. Any partition \theta is also a skew diagram \theta=\theta/(0).

399: Lemma 3.13 .
400: For any partitions \lambda,\mu and any partition \nu\neq\emptyset,
401: \sum_{\lambda,\mu}(-1)^{|\lambda|}c_{\lambda,\mu}^{\nu}s_{\lambda^{\prime}}s_{\mu}=0.
402: Proof.
403: Recall the Hopf algebra structure on \Lambda over \mathbb{Z}. This includes
404: •
405: the usual multiplication map \nabla:\Lambda\otimes\Lambda\to\Lambda with
406: \nabla(s_{\lambda}\otimes s_{\mu})=s_{\lambda}s_{\mu};
407: •
408: the coproduct described previously, with \Delta:\Lambda\to\Lambda\otimes\Lambda with
409: \Delta(s_{\nu})=\sum_{\lambda,\mu}c_{\lambda,\mu}^{\nu}s_{\lambda}\otimes s_{\nu};
410: •
411: the unit \eta:\mathbb{Z}\to\Lambda, the ring homomorphism with 1\mapsto 1;
412: •
413: the counit \epsilon:\Lambda\to\mathbb{Z} taking f\in\lambda to its constant term f(0,0,\ldots);
414: •
415: the antipode S:\Lambda\to\Lambda with
416: S(s_{\lambda})=(-1)^{|\lambda|}s_{\lambda^{\prime}}.
417: The antipode S is characterized by the commutative diagram shown in Figure 4 .
418: Figure 4. The Hopf algebra stucture on \Lambda

420: \displaystyle\eta\circ\epsilon(s_{\nu})

literatureSources.title: Schubert decompositions for ind-varieties of generalized flags
literatureSources.summary: Let $\mathbf{G}$ be one of the ind-groups $GL(\infty)$, $O(\infty)$, $Sp(\infty)$ and $\mathbf{P}\subset \mathbf{G}$ be a splitting parabolic ind-subgroup. The ind-variety $\mathbf{G}/\mathbf{P}$ has been identified with an ind-variety of generalized flags in the paper "Ind-varieties of generalized flags as homogeneous spaces for classical ind-groups" (Int. Math. Res. Not. 2004, no. 55, 2935--2953) by I. Dimitrov and I. Penkov. In the present paper we define a Schubert cell on $\mathbf{G}/\mathbf{P}$ as a $\mathbf{B}$-orbit on $\mathbf{G}/\mathbf{P}$, where $\mathbf{B}$ is any Borel ind-subgroup of $\mathbf{G}$ which intersects $\mathbf{P}$ in a maximal ind-torus. A significant difference with the finite-dimensional case is that in general $\mathbf{B}$ is not conjugate to an ind-subgroup of $\mathbf{P}$, whence $\mathbf{G}/\mathbf{P}$ admits many non-conjugate Schubert decompositions. We study the basic properties of the Schubert cells, proving in particular that they are usual finite-dimensional cells or are isomorphic to affine ind-spaces. We then define Schubert ind-varieties as closures of Schubert cells and study the smoothness of Schubert ind-varieties. Our approach to Schubert ind-varieties differs from an earlier approach by H. Salmasian in "Direct limits of Schubert varieties and global sections of line bundles" (J. Algebra 320 (2008), 3187--3198).

literatureSources.title: On some symplectic quotients of Schubert varieties
literatureSources.summary: Let $G/P$ be a generalized flag variety, where $G$ is a complex semisimple connected Lie group and $P\subset G$ a parabolic subgroup. Let also $X\subset G/P$ be a Schubert variety. We consider the canonical embedding of $X$ into a projective space, which is obtained by identifying $G/P$ with a coadjoint orbit of the compact Lie group $K$, where $G=K^{\mathbb C}$. The maximal torus $T$ of $K$ acts linearly on the projective space and it leaves $X$ invariant: let $Ψ: X \to {\rm Lie}(T)^*$ be the restriction of the moment map relative to the Fubini-Study symplectic form. By a theorem of Atiyah, $Ψ(X)$ is a convex polytope in ${\rm Lie}(T)^*$. In this paper we show that all pre-images $Ψ^{-1}(μ)$, $μ\in Ψ(X)$, are connected subspaces of $X$. We then consider a one-dimensional subtorus $S\subset T$, and the map $f: X\to {\mathbb R}$, which is the restriction of the $S$ moment map to $X$. We study quotients of the form $f^{-1}(r)/S$, where $r\in {\mathbb R}$. We show that under certain assumptions concerning $X$, $S$, and $r$, these symplectic quotients are (new) examples of spaces for which the Kirwan surjectivity theorem and Tolman and Weitsman's presentation of the kernel of the Kirwan map hold true (combined with a theorem of Goresky, Kottwitz, and MacPherson, these results lead to an explicit description of the cohomology ring of the quotient). The singular Schubert variety in the Grassmannian $G_2({\mathbb C}^4)$ of 2 planes in ${\mathbb C}^4$ is discussed in detail.

literatureSources.title: Examples and Counterexamples of Cost-efficiency in Incomplete Markets
literatureSources.summary: We present a number of examples and counterexamples to illustrate the results on cost-efficiency in an incomplete market obtained in [BS24]. These examples and counterexamples do not only illustrate the results obtained in [BS24], but show the limitations of the results and the sharpness of the key assumptions. In particular, we make use of a simple 3-state model in which we are able to recover and illustrate all key results of the paper. This example also shows how our characterization of perfectly cost-efficient claims allows to solve an expected utility maximization problem in a simple incomplete market (trinomial model) and recover results from [DS06, Chapter 3], there obtained using duality.

literatureSources.title: Stable cohomology of universal character varieties
literatureSources.summary: We study the universal PGL_n$character variety over M_g whose fiber over a point [C] is the space of PGL_n-local systems on the curve C. We use nonabelian Hodge theory and properties of Saito's mixed Hodge modules to show that the Leray-Serre spectral sequence for the projection to M_g degenerates at E_2. As an application, we prove that the rational cohomology of these varieties stabilizes as g goes to infinity and compute the stable limit. We also deduce similar results for the universal G-character variety over M_{g,1} whose fiber over a punctured curve is the variety of G-local systems with fixed central monodromy around the puncture, for G = GL_n or SL_n.

literatureSources.venue: The Norm Residue Theorem in Motivic Cohomology
literatureSources.summary: This chapter concerns cohomology operations. Although motivic cohomology was originally defined for smooth varieties over the perfect field 𝑘, it is more useful to view it as a functor defined on the pointed 𝔸 1 -homotopy category Ho · , discussed previously in chapter 12. After defining cohomology operations and giving a few examples, the chapter turns to an axiomatic treatment of the motivic Steenrod operations. The motivic Milnor operations are then presented. Thereafter, this chapter demonstrates that the sequence of Milnor operations 𝑄 𝑖 is exact on the reduced cohomology of the suspension Σ‎𝔛 attached to a Rost variety 𝑋, using the degree map 𝑡 𝒩 . It concludes with Voevodsky's motivic degree theorem.

literatureSources.title: Presenting the cohomology of a Schubert variety
literatureSources.summary: We extend the short presentation due to [Borel '53] of the cohomology ring of a generalized flag manifold to a relatively short presentation of the cohomology of any of its Schubert varieties. Our result is stated in a root-system uniform manner by introducing the essential set of a Coxeter group element, generalizing and giving a new characterization of [Fulton '92]'s definition for permutations. Further refinements are obtained in type A.

literatureSources.title: Schubert puzzles and integrability II: multiplying motivic Segre classes
literatureSources.summary: In Schubert Puzzles and Integrability I we proved several"puzzle rules"for computing products of Schubert classes in K-theory (and sometimes equivariant K-theory) of d-step flag varieties. The principal tool was"quantum integrability", in several variants of the Yang--Baxter equation; this let us recognize the Schubert structure constants as q->0 limits of certain matrix entries in products of R- (and other) matrices of quantized affine algebra representations. In the present work we give direct cohomological interpretations of those same matrix entries but at finite q: they compute products of"motivic Segre classes", closely related to K-theoretic Maulik--Okounkov stable classes living on the cotangent bundles of the flag varieties. Without q->0, we avoid some divergences that blocked fuller understanding of d=3,4. The puzzle computations are then explained (in cohomology onlyin this work, not K-theory) in terms of Lagrangian convolutions between Nakajima quiver varieties. More specifically, the conormal bundle to the diagonal inclusion of a flag variety factors through a quiver variety that is not a cotangent bundle, and it is on that intermediate quiver variety that the R-matrix calculation occurs.

For \(\mathfrak S_v=s_{i^j}\), \(J_v\) is generated by the Schur interval above \(i^j\). The source gives two explicit generating families, each of size \(\binom{a+b}{a}\), and conjectures their minimality; it reports verification only for \(r\le4\) and \(n-r\le5\). [source-2@L1354-L1421|claim=formal-document] [source-2@L1495-L1502|claim=formal-document]
Internal finite work proves minimality for \(i=j=p=c=2\): \(J_{2,2}/A_+J_{2,2}\cong\mathbb Z^6\), and both six-element source families give integral bases.

For the next case \(i=j=p=2,\ c=3\), internal work establishes \[ J_{2,3}=\bigoplus_{(2,2)\subseteq\lambda\subseteq(4^5)} \mathbb Z\bar s_\lambda,\qquad A_+=(\bar h_1,\bar h_2,\bar h_3,\bar h_4), \] and proves that all corresponding Pieri rows give the complete degreewise presentation of \(A_+J_{2,3}\).

whatWeKnow: The source defines \[ I_{r,q}=\bigoplus_{\lambda\not\subseteq q^r}\mathbb Zs_\lambda,\qquad \Lambda/I_{r,q}=\bigoplus_{\lambda\subseteq q^r}\mathbb Z\bar s_\lambda. \] [source-2@L1310-L1331|claim=formal-document]

For rectangular \(\mathfrak S_v=s_{i^j}\), the source gives two generating families of size \(\binom{a+b}{a}\) and conjectures both are minimal; it reports verification only for \(r\le4\) and \(n-r\le5\). [source-2@L1380-L1421|claim=formal-document] [source-2@L1495-L1502|claim=formal-document]
Accepted internal work proves the finite case \(i=j=p=c=2\): \(J/A_+J\cong\mathbb Z^6\), and both six-element source families map to integral bases. This establishes no uniform theorem.

For the next case \(i=j=p=2,\ c=3\), accepted internal work establishes \[ J_{2,3}=\bigoplus_{(2,2)\subseteq\lambda\subseteq(4^5)}\mathbb Z\bar s_\lambda, \qquad A_+=(\bar h_1,\bar h_2,\bar h_3,\bar h_4), \] and identifies all corresponding Pieri rows as the complete relation presentation.

whatWeKnow: The source defines \[ I_{r,q}=\bigoplus_{\lambda\not\subseteq q^r}\mathbb Zs_\lambda,\qquad \Lambda/I_{r,q}=\bigoplus_{\lambda\subseteq q^r}\mathbb Z\bar s_\lambda. \] [source-2@L1310-L1331|claim=formal-document]

For \(\mathfrak S_v=s_{i^j}\), the source gives two generating families for \(J_v\), each of size \(\binom{a+b}{a}\), where \[ a=\min(n-r-i,r-j),\qquad b=\min(i,j). \] It conjectures both families are minimal and reports verification only for \(r\le4\) and \(n-r\le5\). [source-2@L1380-L1421|claim=formal-document] [source-2@L1495-L1502|claim=formal-document]

Accepted project work proves the finite case \(i=j=p=c=2\): the indecomposable quotient is torsion-free of rank \(6\), and both six-element source families map to integral bases. This does not establish a uniform theorem.

For the next case \(i=j=p=2,\ c=3\), accepted work establishes \[ J_{2,3}=\bigoplus_{(2,2)\subseteq\lambda\subseteq(4^5)} \mathbb Z\bar s_\lambda,\qquad A_+=(\bar h_1,\bar h_2,\bar h_3,\bar h_4), \] and proves that all corresponding Pieri rows give the complete degreewise presentation of \(A_+J_{2,3}\).

whatWeKnow: For a bigrassmannian \(v\) with \(\mathfrak S_v=s_{i^j}\), the source defines \[ a=\min(n-r-i,r-j),\qquad b=\min(i,j), \] gives two generating families of \(J_v\), each of size \(\binom{a+b}{a}\), and conjectures both are minimal. The source reports checks only for \(r\le4\) and \(n-r\le5\). [source-2@L1380-L1421|claim=formal-document] [source-2@L1495-L1502|claim=formal-document]

The source-grounded Schur presentation is \[ I_{r,q}=\bigoplus_{\lambda\not\subseteq q^r}\mathbb Zs_\lambda,\qquad \Lambda/I_{r,q}=\bigoplus_{\lambda\subseteq q^r}\mathbb Z\bar s_\lambda. \] [source-2@L1310-L1331|claim=formal-document]

Accepted project work identifies \(J_{p,c}\) with the Schur interval \[ \bigoplus_{i^j\subseteq\lambda\subseteq(i+p)^{j+c}}\mathbb Z\bar s_\lambda \] and reduces minimality questions to the integral indecomposables \(J_{p,c}/A_+J_{p,c}\).
The finite case \(i=j=p=c=2\) is established internally: the quotient is \(\mathbb Z^6\), and both proposed six-element families map to integral bases. This proves only that specialization.

For \(i=j=p=2,\ c=3\), accepted work establishes \[ J_{2,3}=\bigoplus_{(2,2)\subseteq\lambda\subseteq(4^5)}\mathbb Z\bar s_\lambda, \qquad A_+=(\bar h_1,\ldots,\bar h_4), \] and identifies all corresponding Pieri rows as the complete relation presentation.

The quotient has the integral Schur basis \[ \Lambda/I_{r,q}=\bigoplus_{\lambda\subseteq q^r}\mathbb Z\bar s_\lambda, \] and \(J_v\) is the Schur interval above \(i^j\). [source-2@L1310-L1331|claim=formal-document]
Canonical project work reduces minimality to computing the indecomposables \(Q=J_v/A_+J_v\) and proving that each proposed family maps to a \(\mathbb Z\)-basis.
The finite case \(i=j=p=c=2\) is established internally: \[ Q\cong\mathbb Z^6, \] and both six-element source families map to integral bases. This does not imply a uniform theorem.

For the next case \(i=j=p=2,\ c=3\), canonical work establishes \[ J_{2,3}=\bigoplus_{(2,2)\subseteq\lambda\subseteq(4^5)}\mathbb Z\bar s_\lambda, \qquad A_+=(\bar h_1,\ldots,\bar h_4), \] together with the complete Pieri-row presentation of every \((A_+J_{2,3})_e\).

whatWeKnow: The main tracked problem from the original source is Conjecture 4.10: minimality of the lower- and right-adjoined integral Schur generating families for \(J_v\subseteq\Lambda/I_{r,n-r}\).
The lower-adjoined family is proved minimal in the 2024 paper [doi:10.1112/jlms.12832, lines 213-235].

The right-adjoined family is also minimal by the project’s accepted conjugation argument: \(\omega(s_\lambda)=s_{\lambda'}\) transports it to the lower family for the conjugated admissible parameters. The paper suggests this transposition but does not state a separate right-family theorem [doi:10.1112/jlms.12832, lines 481-491; 833-840].

Conditionally on the accepted ideal correspondence, conjugation induces \[ J_v/A_+J_v\cong J_{v^\vee}/A^\vee_+J_{v^\vee}, \] preserving grading, integral torsion invariants, and degreewise free ranks.

Exact computation for the conjugate pair \([222,4^5]\) and \([33,5^4]\) gives quotient ranks \[ (1,1,2,1,1,0,\ldots,0) \] in weights \(6,\ldots,20\), with no torsion; hence each quotient is \(\mathbb Z^6\). This is bounded exact evidence from outputs 5b6e59b74af1b386568e8d3014cdef276ec80f89225cf5ba2367c73fa3b0a993.

A sparse complementary-minor certificate exists for \(22\subseteq\lambda\subseteq4^4\), independently deriving unit Smith data without a black-box Smith computation (outputs 11083cba2a0e58c0f6806d6dbca8cb2df9600abf8e2fb2d94fd0ad46ec5ea0f7).
